result:
Two branches share no common ancestor commit → git can't compute a merge base, refuses by default (since 2.9) to avoid accidentally gluing two separate projects together.

Usual cause: `git init` + commit locally, then `git pull` from a remote created with its own initial commit (README/license). Others: wrong remote URL, history rewritten upstream (force-push, `filter-repo`), or merging from a shallow clone (`--depth`) where the common ancestor got cut off.

First check the remote is the right one: `git remote -v`. If the clone is shallow, `git fetch --unshallow` and retry; the error may disappear.

If the histories really are separate and you want both combined:

```
git pull origin main --allow-unrelated-histories
```

(or `git merge origin/main --allow-unrelated-histories` if already fetched). Resolve conflicts (typically README/.gitignore), commit, push.

If the local repo has nothing worth keeping, simpler: re-clone the remote and copy your files in. If the remote's lone commit is the disposable side, `git push --force-with-lease origin main` overwrites it with your local history. That destroys the remote commits, so only do it on a repo nobody else uses.
